claims.text: The onset of yielding is driven by thermally activated, collective dislocation cross-slip.
The cross-slipping defects are super-dislocations operating on {111} planes.
Yielding is not dominated by dislocation nucleation at defects.
Yielding is not dominated by a deformation-induced phase transformation.
Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is solutionized as an FCC single crystal under the proposed initial conditions.
The tested sample is free of pre-existing dislocation loops.
Chemical short-range order and high Peierls barriers facilitate sessile super-dislocation formation and make cross-slip thermally activated.
At low temperature, high lattice friction inhibits easy dislocation glide.
Dislocations use cross-slip to bypass local chemical obstacles.
Increasing temperature supplies the activation energy for cross-slip and consequently lowers the yield stress.
Yield stress is largely strain-rate independent because thermal barrier crossing, rather than dislocation velocity, is rate limiting.
In traditional metals, dislocation multiplication and velocity dominate strain-rate sensitivity.
In FCC high-entropy alloys, short-range order and stacking-fault-energy variations impede dislocation motion.
Yield strength will decrease strongly with increasing temperature while remaining approximately constant over three to four orders of magnitude in strain rate.
No BCC diffraction peaks will emerge during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
Acoustic-emission events will correspond to discrete cross-slip rather than continuous dislocation-nucleation bursts.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to low-defect-density single crystals; grain boundaries and forest dislocations may alter strain-rate sensitivity in other microstructures.
Crystal orientation must be fixed, with [001] and [111] offered as candidate tensile-axis orientations.
Al-containing HEA variants can be prone to FCC-to-BCC phase changes or decomposition.
Distinct BCC reflections or a discontinuous FCC lattice-parameter shift greater than 0.5% at yield are designated as falsifying evidence against a purely cross-slip mechanism.
